title: Kahana vs Google Play Books: A Stack for the Club, Not a Lifetime Catalog
excerpt: Google Play Books is reading, catalogs, tracking, or ebook storefronts. Kahana is clubs and hubs around the books you actually read together.

metaDescription: Google Play Books is reading, catalogs, tracking, or ebook storefronts. Kahana is clubs and hubs around the books you actually read together.

columns.label: Ebook
columns.definition: Yes if you can easily get and consume ebooks on the platform (free or paid) as a first-class product, open, buy, borrow, or read without hunting.

columns.label: Short-form video
columns.definition: Yes if you can easily consume short-form video as a first-class surface (For You, Reels, Shorts).

columns.label: Long-form video
columns.definition: Yes if you can easily watch creator / UGC long-form video (or specialty long video) as a core surface. Course lectures belong under Courses. Hollywood catalogs belong under Series/Films.

columns.label: Series/Films
columns.definition: Yes if you can easily watch series and films as an SVOD / catalog entertainment product.

columns.label: Courses
columns.definition: Yes if you can easily take or browse structured courses as a first-class product.

columns.label: Newsletters
columns.definition: Yes if you can easily read or subscribe to newsletters / creator writing as a first-class product.

columns.label: Audio
columns.definition: Yes if you can easily listen to music, podcasts, or audiobooks as a first-class product.

columns.label: Memberships
columns.definition: Yes if a creator or seller can accept payments from others and make money through the platform, checkout, fan subscriptions, tips, ads, shop, or creator funds. Not only a classic Patreon-style membership product.

columns.label: Community & Messaging
columns.definition: Yes if you can create or join a group, community, or club, including group chats, Groups, subreddits, community tabs, discussion boards, or community feeds. A one-off comment on a single video or listing is not the bar; a durable place for the group to talk is.

columns.label: Storefronts
columns.definition: Yes if the product gives a creator a custom storefront or site that can take the place of building their own website (bio page, creator site, branded shop). Not a shop tab on someone else’s multi-seller marketplace.

columns.label: Marketplaces
columns.definition: Yes if a typical person can search and shop a catalog of offerings from many sellers, courses, books, digital goods, etc. Storefront software (Shopify, WooCommerce) is not a marketplace unless shoppers browse many sellers there.

scaleFacts: Launched in 2010 (as Google eBooks); now operates in 75+ countries.
Over 10 million ebooks and audiobooks available via the bookstore globally.
Often cited at ≈5% ebook market share in the U.S. far behind Amazon and Apple.
Integrates with Google Classroom (distribute ebooks to students, assignments, highlights/notes, export to Docs).

strengths.title: Large, multi-format catalog
strengths.detail: Millions of ebooks, audiobooks, comics, and manga in one app, one of the larger collections available.

strengths.title: Cross-device access
strengths.detail: Read on web, Android, and iOS with synced progress; upload your own PDFs and EPUBs to read across devices.

strengths.title: Integrated with Google ecosystem
strengths.detail: Ties into Google Play, Google account, and Classroom; notes and progress can export to Google Docs for study.

strengths.title: Reading Mode and clear layout
strengths.detail: Default Reading Mode reduces blue light; Material Design separates ebooks and audiobooks with helpful current-read thumbnails.

weaknesses.title: Small market share vs competitors
weaknesses.detail: Around 5% ebook share in the U.S. a minor sales channel compared with Amazon and Apple.

weaknesses.title: Limited formats and clunky uploads
weaknesses.detail: Supports PDF and EPUB but not DOCX, MOBI, or TXT; manual one-at-a-time uploads; uploaded books sometimes fail to appear until the app is reset.

weaknesses.title: Weak customization
weaknesses.detail: Fewer typographic options than competitors, brightness and font size mainly; limited fonts, margins, and layout control.

weaknesses.title: Store-biased UX and weak library management
weaknesses.detail: Recommendations and store content can overshadow owned books; search often surfaces titles to buy rather than personal uploads.

content:
Kahana is a library of curated hubs, Explore, Clubs, and optional Stripe. Google Play Books is reading, catalogs, tracking, or ebook storefronts. They overlap in places and diverge in others.

What each one is

Kahana is built around hubs people can open, Explore so strangers can find them, Aura as scarce daily recognition, and Clubs so discussion outlives a feed. Selling stays optional.

Dive into a world of stories with Google Play Books!

Why this comparison

This article puts Kahana and Google Play Books side by side. It covers what each supports as a first-class product job, key features, and a few research notes so you have a clearer picture of what they are, how they compare, and what you can actually do on each one. It is not a teardown, and it is not a switch-tomorrow pitch.
contentAfter:
What you can do on each

On Kahana you can publish a hub, list it on Explore, discuss it in a Club, grant Aura, and turn on a Stripe paywall when you are ready to charge.

On Google Play Books you can use Ebook, Audio, Memberships, and Marketplaces as first-class product jobs. You need a dedicated reader, a giant store, or social tracking of everything you have ever read.

Using Kahana with Google Play Books

You can use both. Google Play Books keeps doing what it already does well. Kahana is another place to package the work, get discovered, and grow an audience.

Keep the reader or tracker you already use. Put the Club pick, discussion questions, and related files on Kahana so the book is a shared library item, not only a private progress bar.
